newsitem.title: UK: UK government declares war on the work-shy.
newsitem.headline: UK government declares war on the work-shy.

text.p: Young unemployed Britons who refuse one of four options under the government's new welfare-to-work programme risk losing their welfare benefits indefinitely, Employment Minister Andrew Smith said on Thursday.
The four options are a private-sector job, education or training for up to 12 months, work in the voluntary sector or a place on a new environmental taskforce.

Smith told a news conference that a fit unemployed person who refused to take up one of the options would lose his Job Seeker's Allowance (JSA) initially for two weeks and then for another four weeks.
If he continued to refuse, "that sanction can continue for subsequent months," Smith said.
The JSA is worth 38.90 stg a week for single people, 77.15 stg for a couple and 93.08 stg for a couple with a child under 11.
Young unemployed people with extenuating circumstances who refused to take one of the welfare-to-work options would have their JSA reduced by 40 percent, Smith said.
There is no social security safety net for those who lose entitlement to the JSA, but Education and Employment Secretary David Blunkett denied that the sanctions were harsh.
He said able-bodied young people had a duty to go out and earn their living. Laying in bed all day could no longer be an option, he said.
"This is hope, not punishment. This is opportunity, not some sort of Draconian sanction," Blunkett told the news conference.
When the previous Conservative government withdrew welfare benefits for school-leavers aged 16 and 17, the numbers of young people sleeping rough on the streets increased sharply.

But Blunkett, urging reporters to stifle any thoughts of cynicism, said he expected people to take up one of the options, which he said were all of high quality and amounted to a programme of a sort that had never been tried before.
"We do not believe that people will end up on the streets. We believe they'll end up in work," Blunkett said.

The "New Deal" welfare-to-work programme, to be financed by a windfall tax on the excess profits of privatised utilities, was the centrepiece of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's maiden budget on Wednesday.
A total of 3.5 billion stg will be available to fund it over the next four years with the goal of getting 250,000 under-25s off welfare.
A crucial part of the scheme will be a four-month "gateway" programme designed to provide the necessary social skills and advice to enable young people to hold down a job or take up a placement.
"This is a crusade for the nation. We need to mobilise the commitment and interest of those who can help with the New Deal and those who will benefit most from it," Blunkett said.
